2.2 Toughened Glass (Heat Treafed Glass, Tempered Glass. Hardened G/ass ) - Glass, the surface o which has been rapidly cooled from near its softening point, so that after cooling a residua compressive stress remains in the surface and is balanced by tensile stress below the surface. Thic increases the mechanical strength and thermal shock resistance of the glass and also, when it .breaks causes it to shatter into smaller and less angular fragments than an annealed glass. 2.3 `As Drawn' GlassGlass tubing in the `as made state, not having been furnace annealed, containing certain desirable residual stresses, in particular ccmpressicn slress in the outer surface. ant

are silica, soda and lime. Soda-lime 2.4 `Soda-lime' Glass - Glass in which the main constituents glass has a relatively high coefficient of expansion and hence in the annealed state has only little resistance to thermal shock but its strength and thermal resistance can be greatly increased b) toughening. Z.5 Borosi/ica& G/ass-Silicate glass containing boron as a characteristic constituent. Borosilicate alass has a relatively low co-efficient of expansion and hence has considerable resistance to thermal shock. Because it has a low co-efficient of expansion, it does not develop as much stress as soda-lime Jlass under comparable toughening treatment. Because of its higher softening temperature, borosilicate glass withstands higher duty temperatures than does soda-lime glass without de-toughening. Because t has more resistance to corrosion than soda-lime glass, borosilicate glass is recommended for all r*eflex glasses. :!.6 Defects !.7 Corrosion ressel. APPENDIX

A

A-l. Effects of Temperature and Pressure -Limits of working pressure on tubular gauge glasses depend on freedom from stress induced by badly aligned fittings, the length of glass, and the presence of any corrosive conditions. In steaming application,users should establish a permissible fife, dependent on feed water and pressure conditions, which permits no more than half the tubular wall thickness to be corroded away in the area of the gauge cone or packing. Tubular glasses for boilers, and for other vessels where conditions of pressure, temperature and corrosion are similar to those for boilers, should not be longer than 505 mm unsupported or 600 mm supported. For non-steaming conditions, lengths UP to 1000 mm unsupported and 1200 mm supported may be used. Whare a gauge length above these limits is required, it should consist of a combination of shorter glasses. of glass on pressure vessels is sometimes a problem requiring A-2. Corrosion -Corrosion consideration, because of the faster rate of chemical reactions at temperatures and pressures above atmospheric. Borosilicate glass is more resistant than soda-lime glass to attack by hot water and acids. Toughening does not increase the corrosion resistance of glass. For use under severe conditions, for instance in the presence of alkalis where the consequences of failure would be serious, the use of two glasses ( each capable of withstanding the full pressure ) is to be preferred. In boiler practice, the glass is frequently protected by mica alternatively, corrosion may be minimized by control of the fluid circulation. The glass manufacturer should be consulted regarding the possible effect of corrosion on the properties of glass for pressure vessels wherever particularly adverse conditions are likely to be encountered.
